overview: Wadawurrung people maintain cultural responsibilities across inland, coastal and sea Country in western Victoria. Their knowledge and creative practice continue through families, artists and community institutions.

items.text: The Country Plan connects care for land with teachings attributed to Bunjil, including taking only what is needed and respecting knowledge passed through generations.
The plan identifies murnong, tubers and lilies among valued resources, alongside reeds and grasses used for flour, weaving and string.
Trees supply materials for spears, shields and carriers. Ochre, fibres and resin also belong to the community's named cultural resources.
Rivers, estuaries, wetlands and sea Country are linked cultural places. Fish, eels and shellfish form part of the resources the community seeks to care for.
Wadawurrung artists work in weaving, leatherwork, painting, photography and digital media. Music, storytelling and language teaching also sustain cultural expression.
The Traditional Owners corporation was incorporated in 1998 and received Registered Aboriginal Party status in 2009. These dates concern institutions, not the beginning of Wadawurrung people.
The community describes severe harm following colonisation while affirming the survival and renewal of Wadawurrung people and culture.

sources.title: Wadawurrung Traditional Owners: Country Plan Summary 2020
